fire of love.description: Fire of Love is a 2022 independent documentary film about the lives and careers of volcanologists Katia and Maurice Krafft. Directed, written, and produced by Sara Dosa, the film had its world premiere at the 2022 Sundance Film Festival on January 20, 2022, where it won the Jonathan Oppenheim Editing Award.

all that breathes.title: All That Breathes
all that breathes.description: All That Breathes is a 2022 documentary film directed by Shaunak Sen. It is produced by Shaunak Sen, Aman Mann and Teddy Leifer under the banner of Rise Films. The film follows siblings Mohammad Saud and Nadeem Shehzad, who rescue and treat injured birds in India.

the brutalist.title: The Brutalist
the brutalist.description: The Brutalist is a 2024 epic period drama film directed and produced by Brady Corbet, who co-wrote the screenplay with Mona Fastvold. It stars Adrien Brody as a Jewish-Hungarian architect and severely traumatized Holocaust survivor who emigrates to the United States, where he struggles to recover and get his life back on track.

nickel boys.title: Nickel Boys
nickel boys.description: Nickel Boys is a 2024 American historical drama film based on the 2019 novel The Nickel Boys by Colson Whitehead. It was directed by RaMell Ross, who wrote the screenplay with Joslyn Barnes.

challengers.title: Challengers
challengers.description: Challengers is a 2024 romantic sports film directed by Luca Guadagnino and written by Justin Kuritzkes.

godland.title: Godland
godland.description: Godland (Icelandic: Volaða land, Danish: Vanskabte Land, lit. 'Malformed Land') is a 2022 drama film written and directed by Hlynur Pálmason.

saint omer.title: Saint Omer
saint omer.description: Saint Omer is a 2022 French legal drama film written and directed by Alice Diop, and starring Kayije Kagame and Guslagie Malanda. It is Diop's first narrative feature; her other films have been documentaries.

close.title: Close
close.description: Close () is a 2022 coming-of-age drama film directed by Lukas Dhont, co-written by Dhont and Angelo Tijssens, reteaming after their first feature film Girl (2018).

the souvenir.title: The Souvenir
the souvenir.description: The Souvenir is a 2019 romantic drama film written, directed, and co-produced by Joanna Hogg. The film is a semi-autobiographical account of Hogg's experiences at film school. It stars Honor Swinton Byrne, Tom Burke, and Tilda Swinton.

the good the bad and the ugly.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
the good the bad and the ugly.description: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (Italian: Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo, lit. 'The good, the ugly, the bad') is a 1966 Italian epic spaghetti Western film directed by Sergio Leone and starring Clint Eastwood as "the Good", Lee Van Cleef as "the Bad", and Eli Wallach as "the Ugly".
the good the bad and the ugly.wikipedia: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly

red desert.title: Red Desert
red desert.description: Red Desert (Italian: Il deserto rosso) is a 1964 psychological drama film directed by Michelangelo Antonioni, written by Antonioni and Tonino Guerra, and starring Monica Vitti and Richard Harris. Set in Northern Italy, the story follows a troubled woman who is unable to adapt to her environment after an automobile accident.

nights of cabiria.title: Nights of Cabiria
nights of cabiria.description: Nights Of Cabiria (Italian: Le notti di Cabiria) is a 1957 Italian tragicomedy film co-written and directed by Federico Fellini. The film features Giulietta Masina as Cabiria, a kind-hearted sex worker living in Rome and her adventures and misfortunes trying to find happiness.

bob le flambeur.title: Bob le flambeur
bob le flambeur.description: Bob le flambeur (English translation": "Bob the Gambler" or "Bob the High Roller") is a 1956 French heist gangster film directed by Jean-Pierre Melville and starring Roger Duchesne as Bob. It is often considered both a film noir and a precursor to the French New Wave, the latter because of its use of handheld camera and a single jump cut.

celine and julie go boating.title: Celine and Julie Go Boating
celine and julie go boating.description: Céline and Julie Go Boating (French: Céline et Julie vont en bateau: Phantom Ladies Over Paris) is a 1974 French film co-written and directed by Jacques Rivette. The film stars Juliet Berto as Céline and Dominique Labourier as Julie.

jeanne dielman 23 quai du commerce 1080.title: Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles
jeanne dielman 23 quai du commerce 1080.description: Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles is a 1975 art film written and directed by Chantal Akerman, and starring Delphine Seyrig. Distinguished by its long takes, static camerawork, and slice-of-life depiction of domestic labor, the film follows the routine of a widowed mother (Seyrig) over three days.
jeanne dielman 23 quai du commerce 1080.wikipedia: Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles

the human condition i no greater love.title: The Human Condition I: No Greater Love
the human condition i no greater love.description: The Human Condition I: No Greater Love (第一部 純愛篇／第二部 激怒篇) is a 1959 Japanese epic war drama film directed by Masaki Kobayashi. It is the first part of The Human Condition trilogy.
the human condition i no greater love.wikipedia: The Human Condition I: No Greater Love

jalsaghar.title: Jalsaghar
jalsaghar.description: Jalsaghar (Bengali: জলসাঘর Jalsāghar, lit. 'The Music Room') is a 1958 Indian Bengali drama film written and directed by Satyajit Ray, based on a popular short story by Bengali writer Tarasankar Bandyopadhyay, and starring Chhabi Biswas.

where is the friend s home.title: Where is the Friend's Home?
where is the friend s home.description: Where Is the Friend's House?, is a 1987 Iranian drama film written and directed by Abbas Kiarostami. The plot depicts a conscientious schoolboy's attempt to return his friend's school notebook to his home in a neighboring village, to prevent the friend from being expelled if he fails to hand it in the next day.

y tu mama tambien.title: Y tu mamá también
y tu mama tambien.description: Y tu mamá también (English: And Your Mama Too) is a 2001 Mexican coming-of-age sex comedy road film directed by Alfonso Cuarón, who co-wrote the script with his brother Carlos.

eclipse.title: Eclipse
eclipse.description: L'Eclisse (English: "The Eclipse") is a 1962 romantic drama film co-written and directed by Michelangelo Antonioni and starring Alain Delon and Monica Vitti, with Francisco Rabal, Lilla Brignone, and Louis Seigner.

le cercle rouge.title: Le Cercle rouge
le cercle rouge.description: Le Cercle Rouge (French pronunciation: [lə sɛʁkl ʁuʒ]; "The Red Circle") is a 1970 French crime film written and directed by Jean-Pierre Melville. It stars Alain Delon, Bourvil, Gian Maria Volonté, François Périer and Yves Montand.

the hour glass sanatorium.title: The Hour-Glass Sanatorium
the hour glass sanatorium.description: The Hourglass Sanatorium (Polish: Sanatorium pod klepsydrą) is a 1973 Polish drama film directed by Wojciech Jerzy Has, starring Jan Nowicki, Tadeusz Kondrat, Mieczysław Voit, Halina Kowalska and Gustaw Holoubek.

the fireman s ball.title: The Fireman's Ball
the fireman s ball.description: The Firemen's Ball (or Fireman's Ball; Czech: Hoří, Má Panenko: "Fire, My Lady") is a 1967 Czechoslovak New Wave satirical comedy directed by Miloš Forman. It is set at the annual ball of a small town's volunteer fire department, and the plot portrays a series of disasters that occur during the evening.

magnificent obsession.title: Magnificent Obsession
magnificent obsession.description: Magnificent Obsession is a 1954 American melodrama film directed by Douglas Sirk and starring Jane Wyman, Rock Hudson, and Barbara Rush. It is a remake of the 1935 film, starring Irene Dunne and Robert Taylor.

existenz.title: Existenz
existenz.description: Existenz (stylized as eXistenZ) is a 1999 science fiction horror film written, produced and directed by David Cronenberg. The film follows Allegra Geller (Jennifer Jason Leigh), a game designer who becomes the target of assassins while playing a virtual reality game of her own creation.

in a year of 13 moons.title: In a Year of 13 Moons
in a year of 13 moons.description: In a Year of 13 Moons (German: In einem Jahr mit 13 Monden) is a 1978 West German drama film written, produced and directed by Rainer Werner Fassbinder. It stars Volker Spengler, Ingrid Caven, Gottfried John, Elisabeth Trissenaar, Eva Mattes and Günther Kaufmann.

la chimera.title: La chimera
la chimera.description: La chimera (Italian: [la kiˈmɛːra]; lit. 'The chimera') is a 2023 comedy-drama film written and directed by Alice Rohrwacher. It is set in Italy in the 1980s in a small town on the Tyrrhenian Sea and stars Josh O'Connor as a British archaeologist-turned-grave robber with a gift for divining the locations of Etruscan tombs.

edges.b: star wars episode iv a new hope
edges.claim: Lucas took the trick of telling a war story from the two most powerless people in it — here, squabbling peasants; there, two droids.
edges.attribution: Lucas, repeatedly in interviews and the Star Wars production histories

edges.claim: Tarkovsky thought Kubrick's version of space was cold and phoney, and answered it with a station full of water, grief and clutter.
edges.attribution: Tarkovsky, Sculpting in Time, and contemporaneous interviews

edges.claim: Nolan built from it openly: a silent slab of a machine as the crew's companion, and a final act that abandons physics for a room outside time.
edges.attribution: Nolan in press interviews around the 2014 release

alsoRecord.claim: Both turn on space station, astronaut and space travel.

edges.claim: Villeneuve has named it as the model: an outsider absorbed into a desert people, filmed so the landscape dwarfs the politics.
Boyle sent a crew toward a sublime object with a talking ship for company, and has been open about where the shape came from.
edges.attribution: Boyle in interviews and the Sunshine production commentary

alsoRecord.claim: Both turn on space mission, space travel and suspenseful.

edges.claim: A fenced-off zone that rewrites whoever walks into it, entered by a small expedition that will not come back whole.
edges.attribution: Garland has cited Tarkovsky as a direct influence

edges.claim: A man who cannot stop rebuilding a woman he lost — dressing her double in the same clothes, staging the same encounter again.
Both men design a private architecture whose real purpose is to keep meeting the dead woman inside it.
A manufactured woman built to be someone's company, and a film that keeps asking whether that makes her less real.
Time travel used as a description of memory: the traveller keeps arriving at the same face and cannot get past it.
Falling for someone by watching their room — courtship conducted almost entirely as surveillance from a fixed vantage.
Two strangers adrift in a loud city, the film built from near-misses at food counters and hotel bars rather than from a plot.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are about fleeting relationship.

edges.claim: The city taken in as texture — signage, crowds, snatched glimpses — with a voice over the top turning it into memory.
Lenses so wide the rooms bend, everybody crammed to the edges of a frame that has too much stuff in it.
Young people committing violence in a city shot like a nightclub, the camera closer to them than the film's judgement is.
A night city where neon and rain are the only weather, and every interior is lit by somebody else's sign.
A love affair conducted almost entirely in transit — rented rooms, stations, borrowed time — and narrated from after it ends.

edges.b: portrait of a lady on fire
edges.claim: A relationship told from inside its own ending, so every scene arrives already shaped like a memory of itself.
A parent and child circling something neither will say, staged in still domestic rooms the camera refuses to leave.
A man organising his whole life around a woman who is partly invented, and a film that lets him.
Mastery as a closed craft passed between rivals, with the secret technique withheld from us as long as possible.
Fighting filmed as inherited discipline — schools, lineages, a technique with a history — rather than as spectacle.
A swordsman for hire who sells himself to both sides of a feud and keeps the profit, filmed with no interest in his heroism.

edges.b: once upon a time in the west
edges.claim: A genre slowed to a crawl and turned elegiac: faces held enormous against empty land while almost nothing happens.

edges.b: the good the bad and the ugly
edges.claim: Mercenaries drifting through a desert with no cause between them, the landscape doing the moral commentary.
The climax is a refusal: someone gives up the life they want, and the camera stays politely outside the grief.

edges.b: portrait of a lady on fire
edges.claim: A woman's future settled by family arrangement, filmed as a series of quiet rooms she is placed in rather than chooses.
A life measured near its end, told through small administrative errands rather than through any dramatic reckoning.
Two 1950s Japanese films on the same subject from opposite temperaments: a woman's worth negotiated by everyone but her.

alsoRecord.claim: Chieko Higashiyama and Ichirō Sugai both appear in both films.

edges.claim: A woman politely present at gatherings she has no stake in, the film noticing her drift before she does.
A family photographed at table height, its slow dispersal registered in who is sitting where.

alsoRecord.claim: Yasujirō Ozu directing; Yūharu Atsuta shooting; Yasujirō Ozu and Kōgo Noda writing on both.

edges.claim: A long fall from status told as a series of expulsions, each one filmed at a greater distance than the last.

edges.b: portrait of a lady on fire
edges.claim: A life narrated through the men who trade over her, answered by a film in which the looking belongs to the women.
Two 1950s films arriving separately at the same man: elderly, decent, and quietly surplus to the city he helped rebuild.
Classical ghost stories staged against painted skies — the supernatural handled as theatre design rather than as effect.
Dread built from colour and ceremony: long corridors, saturated artificial light, a haunting that takes its time.
A bounded place that reorganises the person trapped in it until escaping stops being the point.
The location is the antagonist — sand or hotel — and the film is mostly the slow discovery that there is no outside.
A family taken apart by power, filmed in wide static shots that decline to come closer for the suffering.
A film that changes genre at the midpoint, abandoning the room it built to follow the city underneath it.
Shakespeare relocated to Japanese feudal war, with weather and fog doing the work of soliloquy.

alsoRecord.claim: Akira Kurosawa directing; Asakazu Nakai shooting; Akira Kurosawa cutting; Akira Kurosawa writing on both.

edges.claim: A man walked toward his fate through fog or corridors by a building that seems to know the ending first.

edges.b: the good the bad and the ugly
edges.claim: The bored, scratching, entirely unromantic gunman — a hero written as an inconvenience to everyone around him.
Tokyo as a place that keeps overwriting itself, watched by someone trying to hold onto what it used to be.
The person you thought was the protagonist is killed early, and the film continues without a guide in a hostile building.
An ordinary place people go to relax made permanently unsafe, with the threat withheld until the audience supplies it.
Watching as method: a man who solves the problem by observing obsessively, and the film adopting his exact vantage.
Someone hauled across a landscape by an agency that will not explain itself, adjusting from bewilderment to complicity.

edges.b: once upon a time in the west
edges.claim: A wide-open nowhere, a very long wait, and violence arriving into an empty frame the film has made us study.
A man building a scenario in which to keep meeting the woman whose death he caused, and calling it work.
Circling one remembered scene until he walks into it and finds it was always his own death he was remembering.
The state as choreographer: bodies moved in formation through architecture built to make them look small.
Institutional cruelty delivered cheerfully, with paperwork and pop music where the horror should be.

alsoRecord.claim: Both turn on great britain, audacious and satire.

edges.claim: An emptied Britain shot in real streets, the familiar made strange by nothing more than absence.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are set in London.

edges.claim: A space with rules of its own that the men inside keep testing, filmed in long takes that make the walking the story.
The city as one enormous machine, with a clerk lost somewhere in its ducts and the machinery given the best shots.
A man buried in a task that cannot be completed, whose absurdity the film treats with total procedural seriousness.
Two self-serving accounts of the same events, with the film refusing to say which notebook is lying.
A demonstration staged for one spectator, where the real trick is what the demonstrator wants from the watching.
A dead wife who keeps manifesting inside the mission and sabotaging it, because the man cannot let her stay dead.
Grief treated as something with physical reach, and the reunion staged in a room that cannot exist.
Memory assembled as essay rather than story, with the voice and the images deliberately out of step.
Memory as a handful of still images returned to over and over, until the returning is the plot.
A family remembered in fragments, with the camera lingering after everyone has left the room.
Skilled work carried on inside historical violence — the craftsman's discipline against a countryside being burned.
A medieval epic where the spectacle of war is staged at enormous cost in order to be found meaningless.
An epic whose subject withdraws into silence, the scale of the production turned against its own hero.
First contact treated as a problem of grief rather than of technology; the alien mostly returns your own losses.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are about first contact fiction.

edges.claim: The city as a vertical diagram of class — light and towers at the top, the labour that runs it hidden underneath.
The artificial woman built to be tested by the man who made her, with the testing becoming the film's whole structure.

edges.b: star wars episode iv a new hope
edges.claim: The humanoid machine given the most expressive face on screen; the gleaming false Maria is the shape C-3PO inherits.
The interview as the central form: a person questioning a machine to decide whether it counts as one.
The most human speech in the film is given to the artificial mind, and staged as its death.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are about artificial intelligence.

edges.claim: The creature kept out of frame, a small crew picked off one at a time inside a vessel nobody can leave.
A working crew rather than heroes, undone in corridors by something the film keeps mostly off-screen.

alsoRecord.claim: Both turn on space suit, space marine and space travel.

edges.claim: A squad assembled and introduced one skill at a time, then dug into a fixed position against numbers they cannot beat.
The newcomer taken into a professional unit's operation and slowly realising the mission is not the one described.

edges.a: close encounters of the third kind
edges.claim: First contact as awe, answered by first contact as work: the light show replaced by the grind of translation.

alsoRecord.claim: Both turn on alien language, alien contact and extraterrestrial technology.

edges.a: close encounters of the third kind
edges.claim: Contact staged as a religious event — light, scale, silence — with the human characters reduced to witnesses.
A public place emptied by a threat the authorities will not name, filmed with documentary flatness.

edges.b: star wars episode iv a new hope
edges.claim: A desert planet, a chosen adolescent, a mystical order behind the throne — the same furniture, arranged more soberly.

alsoRecord.claim: Both turn on empire, space opera and space.

edges.claim: A man attended by a companion who may be a projection of what he needs, and a film that declines to settle it.

edges.b: the good the bad and the ugly
edges.claim: A border filmed as a lawless middle where three parties want incompatible things and none of them is clean.
A bureaucracy in charge of a catastrophe, filmed with the same cluttered wide lenses that make institutions look mad.

alsoRecord.claim: Terry Gilliam directing; Roger Pratt shooting on both.

edges.a: star wars episode v the empire strikes back
edges.claim: A retreat across hostile country with the party split up, much of it seen from its least powerful members.

edges.b: star wars episode iv a new hope
edges.claim: The recruitment sequence as a genre engine: each member introduced through one demonstration of what they can do.
Memory presented as unreliable testimony, the images quietly withholding what the narration insists on.
Two people thrown together in a hotel, the whole film built out of the corridor between their rooms.

edges.b: portrait of a lady on fire
edges.claim: The withheld glance answered by a look returned directly — longing made mutual instead of missed.
The still, waist-height interior as the shape of everything the characters have decided not to say.
The same encounter restaged again and again, with costume changes standing in for a confession neither will make.
The camera tracking sideways past screens and partitions that hide the face exactly when it matters most.
Restraint used as structure: an affair conducted entirely in public meeting places and never once acted on.
Both films get their subjects to act their own lives for the camera — and both are most revealing exactly where the performance shows.
Two 1920s films inventing opposite documentary instincts: one builds a story out of real life, the other shows you the machinery doing the building.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are silent film, made 7 years apart.

edges.claim: A city cut to music with nobody speaking, the day assembled out of rhythm rather than narration.
The wordless montage taken worldwide: faces, labour and machinery rhymed across places that never share a scene.
The same instrument — time-lapse crowds, aerial landscape, no dialogue — turned from indictment toward awe.

alsoRecord.claim: Ron Fricke shooting; Ron Fricke writing on both.

edges.claim: Reenactment used as evidence: the crime staged repeatedly, each version exposing what the last one wanted to leave out.
A real case reopened by having the actual people replay it, until the replay becomes the more truthful record.
Iranian cinema turning its own restrictions into form — a film about whether what you are watching counts as a film at all.
Opposite ethics for filming atrocity: one refuses every reconstruction and stays on the speaking face, the other hands the perpetrators a camera.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are documentary film.

edges.claim: Handheld, available light, no interviews — the filmmaker simply present until people forget to perform.
The director turns the camera on themselves and lets the announced subject drift, until the digression is the film.
A film assembled around a subject who was already filming himself, and which has to decide what to do with his performance.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are documentary film, made 7 years apart.

edges.claim: The documentary that admits on screen that it is manipulating you, and dares you to keep trusting it.
Documentary built like a heist thriller: reconstruction, score and withheld information used to generate suspense about a known outcome.
A tiny figure very high above a city street, and a film that will not let you stop thinking about the drop.
Years of ordinary time in a Black American neighbourhood, filmed without an engine of plot to hurry it along.
Keaton against a machine too big to argue with — a locomotive, then a cyclone — with the gag and the danger performed in the same unbroken shot.

alsoRecord.claim: Devereux Jennings shooting; Sherman Kell cutting on both.

edges.claim: The stunt done for real and held in wide shot, because cutting away would be the same as admitting it was faked.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are romantic comedy film, made 3 years apart.

edges.claim: A whole film staged as one pursuit along a single line of travel, with the geography kept legible enough that you always know who is gaining.
The modern building treated as an antagonist: a man defeated less by people than by doors, surfaces and machines that were designed without him in mind.
Sound arrives and the tramp still will not speak — the silence kept deliberately, as the last thing that makes him himself.

alsoRecord.claim: Charlie Chaplin directing; Roland Totheroh shooting; Charlie Chaplin cutting; Charlie Chaplin scoring; Charlie Chaplin writing on both.

edges.b: jeanne dielman 23 quai du commerce 1080 bruxelles
edges.claim: The fixed wide shot that refuses to tell you where to look, leaving you to find the event somewhere in the frame.
The city composed as glass, grid and traffic, with people reduced to something moving through the architecture.
A voice reading letters over footage of a city, until the images stop being the place and become somebody's memory of it.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are documentary film, made 7 years apart.

edges.b: jeanne dielman 23 quai du commerce 1080 bruxelles
edges.claim: Duration as the subject: the shot held long past the point of information, so that waiting becomes what the film is about.

alsoRecord.claim: Chantal Akerman directing; Babette Mangolte shooting; Chantal Akerman writing on both.

edges.b: jeanne dielman 23 quai du commerce 1080 bruxelles
edges.claim: A single unbroken take of someone eating, held so long that boredom turns into dread.
A cut that jumps across centuries in one move, and a figure left watching time from outside it.
Non-professional actors, real streets, and a plot that refuses to arrive — the drama is simply that work is scarce and the days keep coming.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are art film.

edges.claim: Working-class childhood filmed in documentary light, where the small private escape matters more than any story about escaping.
A boy and an adult failing him, filmed so plainly that the ending lands as fact rather than as tragedy.
Black American life filmed as texture, weather and silence between people, rather than as incident.
Black independent film built out of images and music instead of plot, and trusting you to assemble the rest.
Saturated colour and slowed, half-ceremonial movement used to give ordinary Black life the weight of myth.
The family that quietly consumes the one member who keeps it going, filmed without ever naming the cruelty as cruelty.
Post-war poverty as an everyday condition rather than a crisis, with melodrama used to make the economics feel personal.
A house that offers no safety, shot cheaply enough to look like footage, ending with a survivor and no relief at all.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are gothic horror film, made 6 years apart.

edges.claim: American horror where the real threat is the country the Black protagonist has to survive, and the arriving authorities are the worst of it.

alsoRecord.claim: Get Out is recorded as based on Night of the Living Dead.

edges.claim: The siege where the dead are a pressure and the other survivors are the argument — the door held shut from both sides.
A long, almost mundane first half that makes the second unbearable, because you were never told which film you were in.
The film that changes genre halfway and strands you, having spent its first hour teaching you the wrong rules.
Italian horror as designed atmosphere — fog, architecture and cruelty staged for beauty rather than for plausibility.
Slow domestic unease turning, without a clean seam, into sustained physical horror.

alsoRecord.claim: Jun Kunimura appears in both films.

edges.claim: Two westerns a year apart that stop to ask what the gunfighter is actually for, and cannot answer without losing him.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are western film, made a year apart.

edges.claim: The showdown stripped of glamour: a man too old for it, a town that will not help, and killing shown as sordid work.
A child watching a gunfighter, and a film that knows the watching is how the myth gets passed on.
Suspense generated by a clock rather than by a villain, the film cutting to time passing until waiting becomes unbearable.
The frontier town after the myth has left it, filmed as dust, boredom and a cinema about to close.
Hired fighters recruited to defend a village, each introduced by a demonstration of what he can do, in a film happy to run three hours to do it.

edges.b: once upon a time in the west
edges.claim: The spaghetti western absorbed wholesale: the held close-up, the harmonica-style motif, the villain given an entrance before a line.
Ritual staged flat to the camera, in frames arranged like painted panels, with almost nothing explained to an outsider.

edges.b: long day s journey into night
edges.claim: Dream logic given a hard visual system, so that images repeat and rhyme instead of following one another causally.

edges.a: long day s journey into night
edges.claim: The very long take used to make a journey feel like trespass, time passing in the shot rather than between shots.
African cinema setting inherited myth against the modern world and refusing to resolve which one wins.
Captivity filmed as spiritual test, in close-up and process, with faith treated as a physical act rather than a belief.
The eastern front rendered as endurance in snow and mud, the camera held on a face until war stops being an event and becomes a state.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are partisan film, made 8 years apart.

edges.claim: A film that cuts between eras thousands of years apart and asks you to hold them as one argument.
A death told through incompatible accounts, with the film declining to certify which one happened.
The courtroom shown as a place that manufactures a story, where the persuasive version and the true one need not be the same.
Neo-noir where the investigation keeps uncovering a system rather than a culprit, and solving it changes nothing.
An unsolved provincial killing filmed in cold industrial landscape, with police competence quietly the real subject.
Korean cinema built on an absence — a disappearance that is never confirmed, and a class grievance underneath it.
Two people separated by time trying to reach each other, with the mechanism left deliberately unexplained.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are about time travel.

edges.claim: Identity filmed as something other people keep trying to adjudicate, held together by the camera's steady attention to one face.
Money as a corrosive agent worked through to its end, with the last act stranded in a landscape that will not sustain anyone.
A technician enlarges his own recording over and over, certain a crime is buried in the grain — Coppola moved the idea from a photograph to magnetic tape.
edges.attribution: Coppola has repeatedly named Blowup as the starting point for The Conversation

edges.claim: The scene where a still photograph is pushed past its own resolution, looking for a body the image was never sharp enough to hold.
Surveillance turned back on the watcher: the tape arrives, and the guilt it exposes is the listener's own.
A man who cannot stop listening at the edge of somebody else's life, and is implicated by the act of watching.
A silent-era mansion, a woman the industry finished with who refuses to accept it, and a dead man narrating his own story from the pool.

alsoRecord.claim: Both turn on loss of sense of reality, hollywood and los angeles, california.

edges.claim: Two women alone together whose faces the film eventually merges, until you cannot say which one has been telling it.
A blonde remade as a brunette and a second half that dismantles the first, revealing the romance as one person's rewrite.
A stage act revealed as playback — the singer collapses, the voice keeps going — and dread built out of sound rather than event.

alsoRecord.claim: David Lynch directing; David Lynch writing on both.

edges.claim: A writer drifting through parties thrown by people who peaked decades ago, narrating his own irrelevance with too much style.
A life assembled from witnesses who contradict each other, with the film declining to supply the version that would settle it.
Power photographed in deep focus and low ceilings, the man at the centre framed further and further from everyone in the room.
Post-war border corruption shot in tilted frames and wet streets, with the friend you trusted turning out to be the rot.

alsoRecord.claim: Orson Welles writing on both.

edges.claim: The canted angle and the shadow thrown across a whole wall, used to make a political betrayal feel architectural.
The diary voice-over, the solitary man rehearsing his hands, and an ending that grants a grace the film has not obviously earned.
edges.attribution: Schrader has written and said this repeatedly, in Transcendental Style in Film and in interviews

edges.claim: Crime filmed as procedure — gloves, timing, the same route walked twice — with the face kept deliberately blank throughout.
Long stretches with no dialogue at all, attention held entirely by hands working at a lock and the risk of a sound.
An animal passed between owners as the only innocent thing on screen, and the measure of everyone who handles it.
The professional as an ascetic: an empty apartment, a fixed ritual, and a code that costs more than the job pays.
The heist given in real procedural time, so the theft plays as work rather than as spectacle.
A boat pushing upriver into jungle while its commander detaches from reality, filmed on a shoot that was visibly going the same way.
An impossible object hauled through the jungle by a man who will not be told it cannot be done, with the film itself doing the hauling.

alsoRecord.claim: Werner Herzog directing; Thomas Mauch shooting; Beate Mainka-Jellinghaus cutting; Werner Herzog writing on both.

edges.claim: A person exhibited as a curiosity, and a film that keeps asking whether its own looking is any different.
War as a descent that keeps removing another layer of the world, until the protagonist's face is the only thing left to read.
Someone vanishes early, the search dissolves into landscape, and the film simply declines to ever explain it.
A disappearance left unresolved on purpose, with class resentment quietly supplying the motive the plot withholds.
A body that may not exist, and characters whose interest in finding it quietly evaporates.

alsoRecord.claim: Michelangelo Antonioni directing; Michelangelo Antonioni and Tonino Guerra writing on both.

edges.claim: American crime pictures re-cut with jump cuts and no remorse, then sold back to Hollywood — Penn's film was first offered to Godard and Truffaut.
A boy failed by school and home, ending on his escape held just long enough to become a question rather than a triumph.
The film runs in something close to real time, with the clock, not the antagonist, generating every ounce of the tension.
Memory laid out as architecture — corridors, mirrored rooms, a scene restaged with the furniture moved — and a man insisting it happened.
A voice recounting a love affair over images that keep pulling toward catastrophe, with memory treated as the actual subject.
An essay spoken in the second person over documentary footage, where the commentary quietly becomes the film's real event.
Lovers driving away from a killing into saturated colour, narrating it in a register far too calm for what they have done.
An old man given a deadline and made to audit his own life, the film cutting away to what he cannot fix.
A pastor losing his faith while counselling a despairing man about the end of the world, kept in a cold empty church throughout.

alsoRecord.claim: Both turn on pastor, faith and priest.

edges.a: the passion of joan of arc
edges.claim: The face shot enormous and unadorned for most of the running time, until skin and eyes are carrying the entire argument.
Colour used as a formal system rather than as decor — here a red that floods the cuts, there a palette assigned per panel.
Two women whose personalities swap and bleed into one another in a landscape that stops behaving realistically.

alsoRecord.claim: Both turn on dual personality, duality and identity crisis.

edges.claim: Faith filmed without irony and without proof, staged so plainly that the miracle has nowhere to hide.
A tidy small town and a polite young man, with the film's real business being what is kept in the house behind him.
Evil arriving inside the family home in a nice suit, seen first by the one person nobody will believe.
The camera made complicit — the opening taken from behind the killer's eyes — and the shock moved from a knife to an empty doorway.
A body in a bath, a death faked mid-film, and an audience begged in the marketing not to give away the ending.
edges.attribution: Hitchcock lost the rights to this Boileau-Narcejac novel to Clouzot and bought their next one, which became Vertigo. The dramatic 'beaten by hours' version of the story was popularized by Truffaut; Narcejac later disputed that framing, so the confidence here reflects a real but less cinematic rivalry rather than the more colourful legend.

edges.claim: An isolated crew who cannot tell which of them is still themselves, with the creature's design used to make trust impossible.

alsoRecord.claim: Both turn on spacecraft, space marine and alien.

edges.claim: A signal that rewrites the body of whoever receives it, and a hero who can no longer locate the edge of the broadcast.
Horror routed through a family watching someone they love become something else, one irreversible stage at a time.
Shot in the streets it depicts with faces pulled from them, close enough to the events that it reads as recovered footage.
Resistance shown as grim administration — cells, couriers, executions of your own — with no heroism offered anywhere.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are war film, made 3 years apart.

edges.claim: Political murder filmed as procedure and paperwork, the investigation's rigour making the eventual cover-up worse.

edges.a: investigation of a citizen above suspicion
edges.claim: A state that cannot be embarrassed: the culprit is known early, and the film's subject becomes the machinery that protects him.
Soviet war film handing the camera to the subjective experience — the spinning sky, the face that stops registering — instead of to strategy.

alsoRecord.claim: Both are war film.

edges.claim: Sirk's widow-and-younger-gardener scandal rebuilt in Munich with a Moroccan labourer, keeping the framing devices and swapping class shame for racism.
edges.attribution: Fassbinder wrote at length about Sirk and named this film as the model

edges.claim: A woman's rise through a wrecked economy, told so that her competence and her damage cannot be separated.
The liberal circle that welcomes an outsider warmly and keeps appraising him, with the politeness itself as the horror.
An invisible figure standing in rooms with people who cannot see it, listening to thoughts it has no way to answer.
A city heard as overlapping interior monologue, the film assembling a place out of what people are privately thinking.
A man who has rebuilt a woman in his head speaking to the real one through glass, unable to look at her while he says it.
A face learning to perform a person, filmed until the imitation starts producing the feeling it was faking.
Long wordless passages in abstract black space, used to make the human body look like an unfamiliar object.
A writer alone in an enormous hotel that will not let him work, with the corridor and the wallpaper doing most of the talking.
A rented room rendered as a state of mind, dread supplied almost entirely by sound and by things seeping through the walls.
A man moving through a crowd of people who all want something from him, the film staged as procession rather than as plot.

alsoRecord.claim: Federico Fellini directing; Leo Catozzo cutting; Nino Rota scoring; Federico Fellini, Ennio Flaiano, Tullio Pinelli and Brunello Rondi writing on both.

edges.claim: Memory of a town played as pageant — exaggerated, affectionate, and openly unreliable about its own past.
The same structure transposed to the border: a village hires gunmen, each recruited in one scene that shows what he can do.

alsoRecord.claim: The Magnificent Seven is recorded as based on Seven Samurai.

edges.claim: A stranger playing two criminal factions against each other in a dead town, close enough that it prompted a lawsuit.

alsoRecord.claim: A Fistful of Dollars is recorded as based on Yojimbo.

edges.a: once upon a time in the west
edges.claim: The doorway shot and the man who cannot be let indoors — the western admitting its hero has no place in the town he saves.
Hired fighters defending a village, restaged for a different national cinema and stretched to fit its own star system.
One woman dressed and coached into becoming another, and a film that treats the remaking as an act of violence.
American racism written as social comedy that keeps almost passing for friendliness, right up until it does not.

edges.b: the discreet charm of the bourgeoisie
edges.claim: Dinner guests who cannot leave, and later guests who can never manage to eat — one absurd rule imposed on polite society and followed to the end.

alsoRecord.claim: Luis Buñuel directing; Luis Buñuel writing on both.

edges.claim: Wealthy people trapped by architecture and etiquette, filmed so that the room's logic outranks anyone's intentions.
Fantasy and waking life cut together with no seam offered, and no scene marked as the one that really happened.

edges.b: the discreet charm of the bourgeoisie
edges.claim: Charity and good manners staged as the joke, with a banquet composed to blaspheme the painting it is quoting.

alsoRecord.claim: Luis Buñuel directing; Luis Buñuel writing on both.

edges.claim: A respectable spouse drawn into a masked erotic ritual, filmed coolly enough that desire looks like a formal system.
The army as an administrative machine that consumes its own men, with the film's fury reserved for officers rather than for the enemy.

alsoRecord.claim: Stanley Kubrick directing; Stanley Kubrick writing on both.

edges.claim: The trench and the tracking shot: the camera walking a line of men to make the scale of the waste physical rather than statistical.
A heist assembled from each man's hour, the timeline doubled back so you watch the same minutes from another pair of hands.
Institutional catastrophe played as deadpan comedy, with the most reasonable-sounding man in the room the most dangerous.
Period filmed as a set of rules rather than a costume: candlelight, slow zooms out, and a narrator who tells you the ending early.
Available light pushed to its limit — candles, magic hour — so the period looks lit by its own century.
